# Chronic kidney disease

> *In Singapore, chronic kidney disease is mostly a complication of diabetes, and as kidney
> function declines, intake has to be matched to what the kidney can still excrete. We cover what
> accumulates as function falls, medical nutrition therapy and why public advice such as eating more
> potassium can become dangerous, and when to refer.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain how the loss of nephrons leads to the build-up of sodium, water, potassium, phosphate,
  acid and urea, and why intake must then be matched to what the kidney can still excrete.
- Classify CKD risk from its cause, eGFR and albuminuria on the heat map, and recognise that
  high-risk CKD makes the diet dietitian-led.
- Explain why protein advice reverses at dialysis, and why unsupervised restriction risks
  protein-energy wasting.
- Recognise where population advice (more potassium, a potassium salt substitute, the DASH pattern)
  becomes hazardous in advanced CKD, and explain why star fruit must be avoided completely.
- Explain why phosphate additives in processed foods matter more than the phosphorus number on the
  label.
- Reinforce sodium reduction, the one dietary change whose advice does not reverse in CKD, and recognise
  when to refer to a renal dietitian.
:::

## Chronic kidney disease at a glance {#sec-overview}

**Chronic kidney disease (CKD)** is long-term damage to the kidneys, usually with a gradual loss of
their function. It is the kidney complication of the disease process that links obesity, type 2 diabetes and
cardiovascular disease (together, the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome), and it shares their risk factors (see the
[*Obesity & metabolic syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd),
[*Type 2 diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd) and
[*Cardiovascular disease & hypertension*](cardiovascular-disease-hypertension.qmd) chapters). CKD is
common, largely silent (detected by blood and urine tests, not symptoms) and progressive
[@kdigo2024ckd]. In Singapore it is mostly a consequence of diabetes, which drives roughly 2 in 3 new
cases of kidney failure [@nkfsKeyStats; @ho2024stemmingckd].

CKD is defined and staged by its cause and by two measurements. The
**estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)** is an estimate of how well the kidneys filter, in
categories G1–G5; **albuminuria**, protein leaking into the urine, is graded in categories A1–A3.
The two are read together on a colour-coded risk "heat map" that Singapore's national guidance follows
[@kdigo2024ckd; @aceCKD2023]. The goal here is to recognise risk, not to recall thresholds: a low eGFR
with heavy albuminuria means high-risk CKD, and from that point on the patient's diet is a specialist
matter.

Three principles shape nutrition in CKD:

- Most CKD is organ damage caused by poorly controlled diabetes and hypertension, so the most effective
  "renal diet" is good glycaemic and blood-pressure control, years earlier (see the *Type 2
  diabetes* and *Cardiovascular disease & hypertension* chapters) [@ahaCKM2023; @ho2024stemmingckd].
- There is no single "renal diet". Nutrition in CKD is individualised, dietitian-led medical nutrition
  therapy (see the [*Interprofessional practice, referral and looking after yourself*](interprofessional-referral.qmd) chapter).
  It changes with the stage of disease and with **dialysis** (treatment that partly takes over the
  kidney's clearance of wastes and water), including the type of dialysis. A generic diet sheet does not
  replace individual advice [@kdoqi2020nutrition; @aceCKD2023].
- Advice that is healthy for the public can reverse in CKD. Eating more potassium, using a potassium
  salt substitute and following the DASH pattern are each good general advice, and each can become
  dangerous once the kidney can no longer clear a potassium load.

## Pathophysiology: what accumulates as kidney function declines {#sec-ckd-science}

Kidney disease changes which foods a person may eat, whereas heart disease mostly changes how much
of certain foods they should eat. The reason is that the kidney does more than filter: it is the main regulator of the
body's water, electrolyte and acid–base balance. The healthy kidney clears sodium, potassium,
phosphate, acid and water, and it activates vitamin D. (The everyday balance of sodium, potassium and water is in the
[*Micronutrients, hydration and electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapter.)

As functioning **nephrons** (the kidney's filtering units) are progressively lost, the substances they
used to clear accumulate in the blood, each with its own consequence [@kdigo2024ckd]:

- Retained sodium and water raise blood volume and blood pressure, and cause **oedema** (swelling
  from fluid collecting in the tissues).
- Potassium can no longer be excreted freely, so a dietary load that a healthy kidney would clear can
  push blood potassium to a dangerous level: **hyperkalaemia**, which disturbs the heart's rhythm
  [@hunter2019hyperkalemia].
- Phosphate is retained and the failing kidney stops activating vitamin D; together these drive
  **CKD–mineral and bone disease**, a disorder of bone and blood vessels [@kdigo2017ckdmbd].
- The waste products of protein metabolism, acid and urea, build up.

![In health (left) the kidney clears sodium, potassium, phosphate, acid and water and activates vitamin D, so the diet need not manage them. As nephrons are lost in CKD (right), these accumulate in the blood, raising blood pressure and fluid load, risking hyperkalaemia, and driving CKD–mineral and bone disease and acid build-up. Intake of five dietary components (sodium, potassium, phosphate, fluid and protein) must then be adjusted to the patient's stage of disease and dialysis status, through individualised, dietitian-led therapy.](/figures/mechanisms/ckd-diet-levers.svg){#fig-ckd-levers width="92%" fig-align="center"}

The five dietary components in the figure are managed to limit these accumulations, but managing them by
eating less has its own danger. The build-up in the blood of urea and the other wastes the kidney normally
clears is **uraemia**, and it blunts appetite just as illness raises the body's demands. Patients
therefore readily develop **protein-energy wasting**, undernutrition superimposed on kidney
disease, and that risk makes automatic restriction hazardous [@fouque2008pew; @carrero2013pewetiology].
The renal diet has to hold the two dangers, accumulation and wasting, in balance, which is why it is
specialist work.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with advanced CKD eats no more potassium than before. Why can his blood potassium still rise to a dangerous level?
A healthy kidney excretes a dietary potassium load, so intake needs no managing. As nephrons are lost,
potassium can no longer be excreted freely, so the same load accumulates and can cause hyperkalaemia,
which disturbs the heart's rhythm. Intake then has to be matched to what the remaining nephrons can
excrete.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: if a failing kidney cannot clear the waste of protein, why is eating as little as possible not the safe response?
Uraemia blunts appetite while illness raises the body's demands, so people with CKD are already
prone to protein-energy wasting. Reflexive restriction adds to that danger. The renal diet has to
balance accumulation against wasting, which is why a specialist sets it.
:::

## Dietary management: medical nutrition therapy in CKD {#sec-ckd-levers}

Renal nutrition is individualised medical nutrition therapy, so the same food can be encouraged in one patient and limited in another. The plan depends on the stage of disease, on whether the patient is on dialysis and which kind, on their potassium and phosphate blood levels, and on their nutritional state. The KDOQI nutrition guideline recommends that it be delivered by a registered dietitian working closely with the doctor [@kdoqi2020nutrition]. The five dietary components are taken in turn below: protein, sodium, potassium, phosphate and fluid.

### Protein: targets before and on dialysis {#sec-ckd-protein}

Protein is a commonly misunderstood part of the renal diet, because the advice reverses at dialysis.
Before dialysis, protein is modestly restricted to reduce the waste load on failing kidneys; once a patient starts
dialysis, which is itself catabolic and removes protein, the target is raised again
[@kdoqi2020nutrition; @lambert2022kdoqicommentary]. Because the same patient needs opposite advice at
different stages, the clinician recognises that protein needs change with stage and refers the patient instead of
applying a number from memory.

The benefit of restriction is also debated. The large MDRD (Modification of Diet in Renal Disease)
study found only a small, statistically fragile effect on the decline in kidney function in its
primary analysis; the confident conclusion that "protein restriction slows CKD" came from a later
secondary analysis [@klahr1994mdrd; @levey1999mdrd]. A fair interpretation is a qualified benefit,
not a settled prescription.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Is a low-protein diet always good for the kidneys?
The belief follows from the waste-load reasoning above: if failing kidneys clear less of the waste
of protein, less protein seems better. Applied reflexively, it can do real harm. If protein is cut without
safeguarding energy intake and without monitoring, patients, especially older ones, can develop
protein-energy wasting. This defined syndrome of low body and muscle mass, poor intake and abnormal
blood chemistry is common on dialysis (roughly a third to a half of patients) and strongly linked to
death [@fouque2008pew; @carrero2018pewprev; @bonanni2011pewmortality]. Adequate energy is what makes
any protein target safe; without enough energy, muscle protein is broken down for fuel
[@kdoqi2020nutrition]. Protein targets are therefore modest, stage-specific and dietitian-set, and
**unsupervised low-protein advice is unsafe** [@piccoli2023lowprotein] (see the
[*Undernutrition & malnutrition*](undernutrition-malnutrition.qmd) chapter).
:::

### Sodium: advice a generalist can reinforce {#sec-ckd-sodium}

Sodium reduction is the one dietary change a generalist can legitimately reinforce, because the advice
does not reverse in CKD. Cutting salt helps here for the same reasons it helps in hypertension, and it also reduces
albuminuria and lets blood-pressure drugs work better [@kdigo2024ckd; @kdoqi2020nutrition]. The KDIGO
(Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) guideline suggests keeping sodium under about 2 g a day
(roughly 5 g of salt), though the evidence is of low certainty and rests on surrogate measures such as
blood pressure [@kdigo2024ckd]. (The population evidence on sodium and blood pressure is in the *Cardiovascular disease & hypertension* chapter.)

Singaporeans start from a high intake: about 9 in 10 exceed the limit, averaging about 3,600 mg a day, most of
it hidden in soups, sauces and food eaten out [@hpb2023sodium]. In CKD, however, one common way of cutting salt,
the potassium salt substitute, needs particular caution (see
[Potassium: the risk of hyperkalaemia](#sec-ckd-potassium)).

### Potassium: the risk of hyperkalaemia {#sec-ckd-potassium}

For the general public potassium is protective, but in advanced CKD the advice reverses. The WHO
recommends eating more potassium (fruit, vegetables, legumes) to lower blood pressure, and the same
guideline explicitly excludes people whose kidneys cannot excrete potassium [@who2012potassium]. The exclusion exists because, in advanced CKD, a potassium load the healthy kidney would clear can instead accumulate to hyperkalaemia and disturb the heart's rhythm [@hunter2019hyperkalemia]. Even so, the field is moving away from blanket fruit-and-vegetable bans toward individualised, blood-level-guided advice, because whole-food potassium is
handled differently by the body than the number on a label suggests, and over-restriction worsens diet
quality. Individualising the advice is a dietitian's job [@kdoqi2020nutrition; @clegg2020potassiumplant].

The panel below sets five pieces of standard advice against two patients, a healthy adult and someone
with advanced CKD. Toggle the patient to see which advice reverses and which holds.

<div data-island="renal-flip" data-src="/diagrams/renal-flip.yml"></div>

Two hazards carry more risk than an ordinary high-potassium food and should be recognised on sight.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two hazards: the potassium salt substitute and star fruit
**The potassium salt substitute.** "Low-sodium" or "heart-healthy" salt swaps sodium chloride for
potassium chloride. For most people the swap lowers cardiovascular risk: in a large trial it cut
strokes and deaths. That trial excluded people with serious kidney disease and those taking potassium-sparing
diuretics or potassium supplements, so its safety data do not cover CKD, where the swap can precipitate life-threatening hyperkalaemia
[@neal2021ssass; @xu2024saltsubstitutes; @doorenbos2003saltsubstitute]. (The same caveat appears in the
*Cardiovascular disease & hypertension* chapter.)

**Star fruit and belimbing (bilimbi).** Beyond their potassium, these fruits carry a neurotoxin that
healthy kidneys clear but failing ones cannot. In CKD it causes hiccups (the commonest symptom), confusion, seizures and death, with
mortality reported in about a quarter to a third of intoxicated patients with impaired kidney function [@chua2017starfruit;
@caetano2017bilimbi]. For a CKD patient they must be **avoided completely**, not eaten in controlled portions.
The warning matters locally, since both fruits are common in Singapore gardens and juices
[@nkfsEatingRightCKD].
:::

### Phosphate: dietary sources and absorption {#sec-ckd-phosphate}

Retained phosphate silently contributes to CKD–mineral and bone disease, and its form matters more than
the amount [@kdigo2017ckdmbd; @gonzalezparra2012phosphorus]. Phosphate that occurs naturally in
whole foods (meat, dairy, legumes) is only partly absorbed, roughly 40–60%, and less from plant
sources. By contrast, **phosphate additives**, the inorganic phosphates used to preserve and improve processed
foods, are absorbed almost completely, up to about 90–100% [@noori2010phosphorus;
@gonzalezparra2012phosphorus].

![Not all dietary phosphate is absorbed equally. Phosphate bound in plant foods (phytate) is the least available; the phosphate naturally in animal foods is partly absorbed; but the inorganic phosphate *additives* in processed foods are almost completely absorbed, and are often invisible on the label. Preferring fresh over processed, and scanning ingredient lists for "-PHOS" additives, is the practical approach.](/figures/mechanisms/phosphate-absorption.svg){#fig-phosphate width="80%" fig-align="center"}

These additives are often not on the label. "Enhanced" meats and many processed products carry a large
hidden phosphate load, so the printed phosphorus figure greatly underestimates what is actually absorbed
[@sherman2009enhancedmeat; @stjules2017phosphateadditive]. The practical approach is to prefer fresh over
processed foods and to scan ingredient lists for additives ending in "-PHOS"
[@bump2016organicphosphorus; @gutierrez2013phosphateadditives]. Whether a patient then needs a
**phosphate binder** (a drug taken with meals) is a specialist decision [@tsuchiya2021phosphate;
@ketteler2025ckdmbd]. (The calcium and vitamin D physiology behind the bone side of the disorder,
including parathyroid hormone and fracture risk, is in the
[*Bone & joint health*](bone-health-osteoporosis.qmd) chapter.)

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Eating out
The renal-diet hazards in Singapore's food environment are specific and local, and fall into two groups:

| Hazard | Common local sources |
|---|---|
| High potassium | Coconut milk and kaya, durian, bananas, kangkong, dhal, essence of chicken, stock cubes, Milo- or Horlicks-type malt drinks, strong kopi or teh |
| Additive phosphate | Luncheon and canned meat, sausages, meat patties, processed cheese, malt drinks, colas |

Dietitians teach **leaching** (soaking cut vegetables, then boiling them and discarding the water) to
lower their potassium, but the amounts are individualised, so flag these foods and refer rather than
hand out quantities [@nkfsEatingRightCKD].
:::

### Fluid: when restriction is needed {#sec-ckd-fluid}

Fluid restriction is an easy measure to over-apply: early CKD usually needs none [@aceCKD2023];
limits matter mainly in advanced disease and on dialysis, where retained water shows up as weight gain
between sessions, ankle and lung oedema, and breathlessness [@kdoqi2020nutrition]. Even then there is no universal fluid target: it is individualised and set by the renal team. The generalist's part is to
recognise the signs of overload, link thirst to salt intake, and refer, not to prescribe a millilitre
limit.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can a generalist reinforce cutting salt in CKD, but not the public advice to eat more potassium?
Cutting sodium helps in CKD for the same reasons it helps in hypertension, and it also reduces
albuminuria and helps blood-pressure drugs work, so the advice does not reverse. Potassium advice does
reverse: a load the healthy kidney would clear can accumulate to hyperkalaemia in advanced CKD, which is
why the WHO advice to eat more excludes these patients. A dietitian sets the potassium amount according to
blood levels.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient on a modest protein restriction starts dialysis. Why does his protein target go up?
Before dialysis, protein is modestly restricted to reduce the waste load on failing kidneys. Dialysis is
itself catabolic and removes protein, so the target is raised again. Because the same patient needs
opposite advice at different stages, the target is set by the renal dietitian, not applied from memory.
:::

## When to refer {#sec-ckd-refer}

Once CKD is confirmed, individualised nutrition is the treatment, and it is dietitian-led. Refer
whenever the advice needed exceeds general healthy eating; in practice, five findings are useful triggers for a referral, several of which Singapore's ACE guidance also lists as reasons for shared specialist care [@kdoqi2020nutrition; @aceCKD2023]:

- eGFR is falling, or is roughly in category G3b or worse.
- CKD coexists with diabetes.
- Potassium or phosphate blood levels are abnormal.
- There is weight loss or any sign of protein-energy wasting.
- The patient is starting dialysis.

In Singapore the National Kidney Foundation provides most subsidised dialysis and runs the renal
education programmes to which patients are referred [@mohNkfDialysis2026; @nkfsEatingRightCKD]. (The wider
referral map, who does what across the multidisciplinary team, is in the
[*Interprofessional practice, referral and looking after yourself*](interprofessional-referral.qmd) chapter.)

::: {.callout-important}
## You recognise the five components; you do not prescribe the renal diet
You recognise the five dietary components (protein, sodium, potassium, phosphate and fluid), but a
renal dietitian individualises the quantities to the patient's stage, dialysis status and blood results
[@kdoqi2020nutrition; @aceCKD2023]. Your part is to reinforce sodium reduction (the one change that is
safe for a generalist), avoid the two safety hazards (a potassium salt substitute or star fruit in the
wrong patient), watch for wasting, and **refer**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a patient with diabetes and CKD has normal potassium and phosphate levels. Why refer him to a dietitian anyway?
CKD with diabetes is itself a trigger for referral, because the advice he needs exceeds general healthy
eating: his protein, potassium, phosphate and fluid needs change with his stage, dialysis status and
blood results.
:::

## What does a "kidney diet" actually look like? {#sec-close}

It looks like a dietitian's individual plan, not a printed list. A person with early CKD mostly needs
their diabetes and blood pressure controlled and their salt cut: the ordinary heart-healthy plate, done
well. As the disease advances, the diet becomes an individualised balance, adjusted to the person and
their stage:

- enough protein and energy to avoid wasting, but not so much as to overload failing kidneys;
- potassium and phosphate adjusted according to blood levels rather than banned;
- fluid limited only when overload appears.

## The Singapore context {#sec-singapore}

**Diabetes drives most new cases of kidney failure in Singapore.** Singapore has one of the highest
rates of diabetes-driven kidney failure in the world: about 6 people a day start treatment for kidney
failure, over 9,000 are on dialysis, and roughly 2 in 3 new cases are due to diabetes [@nkfsKeyStats;
@leo2020dialysissg]. Local CKD prevalence is closely linked to the cardiometabolic risk factors: it is far higher
in people with diabetes or hypertension than in those without, and is projected to rise toward 1 in 4
residents as those conditions climb [@ho2024stemmingckd; @wong2018ckdprojection]. The largest benefit for
the kidney therefore comes years earlier, from the control of diabetes and blood pressure.

**Diabetes prevention is also CKD prevention.** Because diabetic kidney disease accounts for most
new dialysis starts, the national War on Diabetes is also a central CKD-prevention strategy
[@mohWarOnDiabetes]. This fits the American Heart Association's concept of **cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome**, which treats obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and CKD as one connected disorder [@ahaCKM2023]. Once CKD is established, the guidance from Singapore's Agency for Care Effectiveness (ACE) follows the same heat-map staging and, like the triggers in [When to refer](#sec-ckd-refer), is pragmatic about referral: not every patient needs a dietitian, but referral can help those with more complex dietary needs [@aceCKD2023].

**The renal diet clashes with typical hawker food, and the clash contributes to poor intake.** A low-salt,
potassium-aware, low-additive-phosphate diet conflicts with strongly flavoured hawker food based on soy,
sambal, coconut and preserved dishes. The clash is one reason patients struggle to eat well and develop
wasting, and another reason the plan needs a dietitian who can adapt it to how people eat
[@carrero2013pewetiology].

## Practise: Uncle Lim and the "eat more banana" advice {#sec-case}

Uncle Lim, 62, has diabetic kidney disease and takes an ACE inhibitor. He brings a friend's printout
recommending more banana and a low-sodium salt, and has started skipping meals to keep his protein low.
Work through the visit: classify his risk, handle the potassium advice and the protein mistake safely,
choose the one dietary change you can reinforce, and notice where prescribing a number instead of referring
would be a mistake.
